newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil assured of any CVRD windfalls.
newsitem.headline: Brazil assured of any CVRD windfalls.

text.p: The Brazilian government will ensure that it and minority shareholders get a slice of any mineral windfall discoveries by Companhia Vale do Rio Doce (CVRD) after the mining giant is privatized, officials said.

In newspaper articles vigorously defending the sell-off of the government's 51 percent stake in CVRD, National Development Bank (BNDES) privatization director Jose Pio Borges said debentures would be issued to ensure government income from future mineral discoveries.
The reason for the delay was ostensibly to allow analysts Mineral Research Development Inc (MRDI) time to evaluate new gold and copper finds in the Carajas region of Para state.

Borges said MRDI's findings were identical to those already published in October and again early this month by CVRD, namely that the deposit was "promising" but that it was too early to tell if it could be viably mined.
Critics of the privatization process have gleefully seized on reports of "historic" finds in Carajas, near the Igarape Bahia gold mine and the Salobo gold, copper and silver project.

"In the case of deposits discovered after privatization, at any time and in whatever part of the country where the company has a right to carry out surveys, the government will have the right to a share of the receipts," Borges wrote.
"For this, we will create debentures, special paper which will pay a percentage of whatever income is derived from the deposits," he added.
Teresa Cristina Aquino, privatization superintendent at the BNDES, said in a recent interview with Reuters the debentures would also be valid for current minority shareholders.
They would cover both undiscovered mineral deposits and known deposits which outlive their expected lifetimes or exceed their currently estimated reserves.
"The government has all the guarantees possible to ensure it will not miss out on any fantastic discoveries by CVRD in the future," she said. "Minority shareholders too."
The CVRD sell-off, due to be Latin America's largest and expected to net some $6.0 billion according to Planning Minister Antonio Kandir, was recently put back to April from first quarter 1997.
They say CVRD's minumum price should only be set once those deposits are fully surveyed in three years time and accuse Brasilia of selling off the nation's jewels for a pittance.
But Borges disputed that claim, saying that apart from the debentures, the government would be assured of its fair share through royalties and income tax.
"The issue of mineral rights is being dealt with with the greatest technical rigor. It can't be subject to emotionalism," he wrote.
Brazil's National Privatization Council (CND) is next expected to meet on February 6, if the report by MRDI is completed by then.

Aquino said the CND should be able to set CVRD's base price once it has the study of the Carajas deposits. The privatization of the world's largest iron ore exporter is now expected to begin in April with the block sale of 40-45 percent of voting shares. Staff may be able to participate.
After the block sale, there will be public offerings both nationally and abroad.
